approachQuestion.prompt:
Smallest separation in a sample

A lab records integer measurements in no meaningful order. Return the smallest absolute difference between any two values. The input array belongs to the caller and must be unchanged when your method finishes. Return only the difference.

Constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 200,000; −1,000,000,000 ≤ values[i] ≤ 1,000,000,000. Repeated values are allowed. Arithmetic is exact for these bounds.

Examples:
1. values = [12, -3, 7, 8] → 1 (the pair 7 and 8).
2. values = [-5, -5, 4] → 0.

Choose the method that returns the required result for every allowed input, preserves the caller’s array, and has the best asymptotic worst-case running time in the comparison-based model. In this model, ordering values is done by comparing values; do not use their bounded integer representation for radix, counting, or bucket sorting.
constraints: Input order has no meaning for this result.
The caller-owned values array must not be mutated; any sorting must operate on a copy.
Return one integer; no pair or reordered array is required.

Select the asymptotically fastest worst-case method among the listed valid approaches under the stated comparison-based model; comparison-sorting the copy is permitted, radix/counting/bucket methods are outside this model.

options.text: Copy the values, sort the copy, then scan adjacent entries and keep the smallest gap.
options.feedback: Sorting exposes every closest pair as neighbors in sorted order; working on a copy preserves the caller-owned array.

options.text: Compare every pair of original values and retain the smallest absolute difference.
options.feedback: This returns the correct result and preserves the input, but comparing every pair takes more worst-case comparisons than sorting once and checking adjacent values, so it does not meet the stated optimization goal.

options.text: Sort the caller’s array in place, then scan adjacent entries for the smallest gap.
options.feedback: The numeric answer can be right, but the method violates the explicit no-mutation contract. For [12, -3, 7, 8], sorting changes the caller’s array to [-3, 7, 8, 12].

options.text: Return the largest value minus the smallest value.
options.feedback: The extreme values need not be the closest pair. For [-3, 7, 8, 12], this returns 15 while the required minimum gap is 1.

feedback.reason: The method must satisfy the complete input/output contract, including required order and mutation behavior.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed below—copy the input, use comparison merge sort on the copy, then scan adjacent entries—choose its worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Count the copied array and merge-sort buffer as additional memory; exclude the caller’s input and the one-number result. Arithmetic is constant-time.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) additional space
O(n log n) time, O(1) additional space

feedback.reason: Merge sort orders the copy in the worst case, and the adjacent scan is linear. The copied values and merge buffer are both linear-size, so their combined auxiliary space remains linear. Pairwise comparison is quadratic; constant space omits the required copy/buffer; a linear-time sort is not guaranteed for unrestricted signed integers under this comparison-sort model.

methodReveal.title: Order a working copy, then compare neighbors
methodReveal.description: Make a separate copy of the measurements and sort that copy with comparison merge sort. Scan the ordered copy once, comparing each value with the one immediately before it, and retain the smallest gap. Equal values naturally produce a gap of zero; the original array is never changed.
